paper_a.title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient via Predictive Variance Reduction (Johnson & Zhang, 2013)

paper_b.title: A Stochastic Gradient Method with an Exponential Convergence Rate for Finite Training Sets (Le Roux, Schmidt, Bach, 2012)

metadata.description: SAG and SVRG are concurrent/near-simultaneous discoveries of variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods achieving linear convergence for finite-sum strongly convex optimization. SAG stores per-example gradients and uses their average (biased estimator); SVRG periodically computes a full gradient snapshot and uses it for variance reduction (unbiased estimator). Both achieve the same O((n + kappa) log(1/epsilon)) complexity but with different memory/computation tradeoffs.

matches.explanation: Both define the identical finite-sum optimization problem: minimize $f(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(x)$ where each $f_i$ is smooth convex and $f$ is strongly convex. Same problem setup arising from empirical risk minimization.

Both are variance-reduced stochastic gradient algorithms but with different mechanisms. SVRG: compute full gradient $	ilde{\mu} = 
abla P(	ilde{w})$ at a snapshot point, then use control variate $v_t = 
abla f_{i_t}(w_t) - 
abla f_{i_t}(	ilde{w}) + 	ilde{\mu}$. SAG: maintain table of $n$ stored gradients, update one per step, use their average. SVRG is unbiased and memory-free ($O(d)$); SAG is biased but avoids periodic full gradient computation.

Both prove linear convergence rates of the same order. SVRG: $O((n + L/\mu) \log(1/\epsilon))$ gradient evaluations. SAG: $O((n + L/\mu) \log(1/\epsilon))$ gradient evaluations. The convergence rate is essentially identical, with differences only in constants.

SAG's variance reduction is implicit: stored gradients converge to true gradients at the optimum, so variance vanishes. SVRG achieves variance reduction explicitly through the control variate construction.
SAG's $O(nd)$ memory requirement for storing all $n$ gradients is specific to SAG. SVRG requires only $O(d)$ additional memory (the snapshot gradient), making it preferable when $n$ is large.

SVRG's proof technique bounds the variance of the control-variate estimator using smoothness ($\leq 4L[P(w_t) - P(w^*) + P(\tilde{w}) - P(w^*)]$), a technique specific to the snapshot-based approach. SAG uses a different Lyapunov-based analysis tracking stored gradient errors.

SAG's gradient estimate is biased (stored gradients computed at different past iterates). SVRG's control variate construction is unbiased by design ($\mathbb{E}[v_t] = \nabla P(w_t)$). Despite SAG's bias, both converge linearly.
